title: [1.30.x]  HTTP/3 (QUIC) connections leak? - Active connections grows unbounded
body: ### Bug Overview After upgrading from 1.28 to the 1.30.x branch, stub_status `Active connections` climbs steadily over days/weeks (observed ~500 → ~3000+) and is only ever cleared by a full restart it seems. The growth comes entirely from HTTP/3 / QUIC connections that are never freed; they accumulate in the Waiting state. I tested this by disabling quic on my vhosts and restarting nginx. **With HTTP/3 enabled, comparing stub_status against established TCP on :443:** ``` $ ss -tanH state established '( sport = :443 )' | wc -l 445 # real client concurrency (HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2) $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1/status Active connections: 855 server accepts handled requests 898040 898040 47582264 Reading: 0 Writing: 27 Waiting: 768 ``` - Active (855) is ~2× established TCP (445). - Waiting (768) is larger than the total number of established TCP connections — impossible for TCP keepalive alone, so several hundred "Waiting" connections are idle QUIC connections that were never closed. - This gap grows monotonically over time and only resets on a full process restart. I updated on the 29th of April. Left side is the active conns axis (black line). It slowly creeps up over a timespan of days/weeks. My nginx config has not changed. Zabbix gets this data from the nginx status stub. As you can see it grew to 3000 earlier in the month before I restarted nginx after another `apt upgrade`. Disabling QUIC (commented `listen ... quic reuseport` + removed `Alt-Svc h3` advertisement) and doing a full systemctl restart nginx: ``` $ ss -tanH state established '( sport = :443 )' | wc -l 428 $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1/status Active connections: 463 server accepts handled requests 2197 2197 106700 Reading: 0 Writing: 15 Waiting: 449 ``` Active now tracks established TCP ~1:1 and stays relatively flat. With QUIC re-enabled the gap and unbounded growth return. This only happened after a restart, I did a reload after disabling quic and nothing changed. ### Expected Behavior ~500 active connections shown like before. Similar active/established connection count. ### Steps to Reproduce the Bug ### NGINX Configuration ``` # nginx.conf worker_processes 64; events { worker_connections 65535; multi_accept on; use epoll; } http { keepalive_timeout 65; ... } # vhost listen :443 ssl reuseport; listen :443 quic reuseport; listen [::]:443 ssl reuseport; listen [::]:443 quic reuseport; http2 on; quic_retry on; ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":$server_port"; ma=86400'; # backend is fastcgi_pass 127.0.0.1:9000 (no upstream keepalive) ``` ### NGINX version and build configuration options ``` nginx version: nginx/1.30.2 built by gcc 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) built with OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024 TLS SNI support enabled configure arguments: --prefix=/etc/nginx --sbin-path=/usr/sbin/nginx --modules-path=/usr/lib/nginx/modules --conf-path=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf --error-log-path=/var/log/nginx/error.log --http-log-path=/var/log/nginx/access.log --pid-path=/var/run/nginx.pid --lock-path=/var/run/nginx.lock --http-client-body-temp-path=/var/lib/nginx/client_temp --http-proxy-temp-path=/var/lib/nginx/proxy_temp --http-fastcgi-temp-path=/var/lib/nginx/fastcgi_temp --http-uwsgi-temp-path=/var/lib/nginx/uwsgi_temp --http-scgi-temp-path=/var/lib/nginx/scgi_temp --user=www-data --group=www-data --with-compat --with-file-aio --with-threads --with-http_addition_module --with-http_auth_request_module --with-http_dav_module --with-http_flv_module --with-http_gunzip_module --with-http_gzip_static_module --with-http_mp4_module --with-http_random_index_module --with-http_realip_module --with-http_secure_link_module --with-http_slice_module --with-http_ssl_module --with-http_stub_status_module --with-http_sub_module --with-http_v2_module --with-mail --with-mail_ssl_module --with-stream --with-stream_realip_module --with-stream_ssl_module --with-stream_ssl_preread_module --add-module=/tmp/debbuilder.lM7Y5l/nginx-1.30.2/nginx-module-gps-license-1.1.1 --with-http_v3_module --with-cc-opt='-g -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer -ffile-prefix-map=/tmp/debbuilder.lM7Y5l/nginx-1.30.2=. -flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects -fstack-protector-strong -fstack-clash-protection -Wformat -Werror=format-security -fcf-protection -ffat-lto-objects -Wl,-z,relro -Wl,-z,now' ``` ### Environment where NGINX is being built and/or deployed - Target deployment platform: AMD64 - Target OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS ### Architecture where NGINX is being built and/or deployed `Linux 6.8.0-111-generic #111-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Sat Apr 11 23:16:02 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed report.
  
  Reproduced locally -- it's not a connection refcount leak. After nginx -s reload (what apt upgrade triggers), old workers keep their QUIC reuseport socket open and can't exit while they still hold HTTP/3 connections (QUIC timers aren't cancelable, and worker_shutdown_timeout is unset by default). Each reload that catches in-flight H3 connections leaves another worker generation alive, and stub_status Active sums one shared counter across all of them -- so it climbs until a full restart reaps the processes. Disabling QUIC removes the path, matching what you saw.

  Repro (1.30.2, http/3, reuseport): a slow H3 download active across a reload -> default config: old worker stays shutting down 30s+ later, Active doesn't drop (a 2nd reload stacks another). With worker_shutdown_timeout 5s: workers exit in ~6s, Active returns to baseline.

  Mitigation: set worker_shutdown_timeout (e.g. 30s). Confirm with ps -o pid,etimes,stat -C nginx before a restart -- workers older than your last reload are the lingering ones.

   Thank you again

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Following up after digging into this further.

  First, on the earlier suggestion: since worker_shutdown_timeout 30s didn't change anything for you, the count isn't
  coming from lingering shutdown workers after a reload. The continuous creep you're seeing (rather than step jumps at
  apt upgrade time) points at live workers plus the shared stats zone, so I went looking there.

  I built stock nginx 1.30.2 with HTTP/3 over OpenSSL 3.0.x (the same QUIC compatibility layer your build uses) and
  stress-tested the QUIC connection lifecycle, in both a single-worker setup and a 64-worker reuseport setup matching
  your config (http3 on, quic_retry on, stub_status). I drove it with a real HTTP/3 client and watched Active
  connections across:

  - clean H3 requests with graceful close;
  - connections abandoned without a CONNECTION_CLOSE (client just disappears, like a roaming/NAT client dropping off);
  - Initial-only floods that trigger Retry and never complete (i.e. background internet probe traffic);
  - half-open handshakes dropped before Finished;
  - high connection churn (hundreds of short-lived connections);
  - QUIC connection migration (client changing source port mid-connection, which with reuseport and no eBPF steering
  lands packets on a different worker).

  In every case Active returned to baseline within the idle timeout, and no worker crashed. I could not reproduce
  unbounded growth on a vanilla build. So the core QUIC connection accounting in 1.30.2 looks sound on these paths.

  Given that, two things would narrow this down a lot:

  1. The most useful test: can you reproduce on a stock 1.30.2 built without the
  --add-module=.../nginx-module-gps-license add-module? A vanilla core doesn't leak in my testing, so isolating that
  third-party module (in or out) is the key data point.
  2. Crash check. In error.log, are there any exited on signal or [alert] lines, and do the worker PIDs change over time
  (ps -o pid,etimes,stat -C nginx)? A worker that crashes and respawns leaves its connections' count un-decremented in
  the shared stats zone -- which is recreated only on a full restart, not on reload -- producing exactly the "climbs
  continuously, only a full restart clears it, worker_shutdown_timeout makes no difference" pattern you describe.

  One more datapoint that distinguishes a real leak from a stats discrepancy: does worker memory (RSS) grow alongside
  Active, or stay flat? Growing RSS points to a real connection/object leak; flat RSS with climbing Active points to a
  counter-accounting issue (most likely a crashed worker, per above).

  If the growth persists on a vanilla 1.30.2 without the add-module, please share that and I'll dig further -- but right
  now the evidence points to either the third-party module or worker crashes rather than the core QUIC code.

comments.body:
Update with coredump / GDB findings. Previous reply got a bit messy with all the editing :-) As I have only a slight clue of what the hell this means I had GPT summarize the important bits. Hopefully it saves you some time.

**Relevant context:**

1. Problem started after upgrading from nginx 1.28.x to the 1.30.x branch.
2. With QUIC disabled and nginx fully restarted, Active connections stayed stable.
3. With QUIC enabled, Active connections slowly climbs and workers segfault.

**Current version/build:**

```text
nginx version: nginx/1.30.3
Package: nginx 1.30.3-1~noble from nginx.org/packages/ubuntu noble/nginx
OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS amd64
built with OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024
runtime OpenSSL: OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024
configure includes: --with-http_v3_module
```

**Loaded dynamic modules in the crashed worker:**

```text
/usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_brotli_static_module.so
/usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_brotli_filter_module.so
/usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_zstd_static_module.so
/usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_zstd_filter_module.so
```

**Two recent coredumps:**

```text
Wed 2026-07-08 14:03:22 CEST 422111 SIGSEGV /usr/sbin/nginx
Wed 2026-07-08 14:24:21 CEST 423749 SIGSEGV /usr/sbin/nginx
```

Both had the same stack shape.

**Backtrace with nginx debug symbols:**

```text
#0  __memset_avx512_unaligned_erms ()
#1  BUF_MEM_grow_clean () from /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcrypto.so.3
#2  ?? () from /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.3
#3  ngx_ssl_handshake (c=0x74b5746248c8) at src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c:2219
#4  ngx_ssl_handshake (c=0x74b5746248c8) at src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c:2213
#5  ngx_ssl_handshake_handler (ev=<optimized out>) at src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c:2561
#6  ngx_epoll_process_events (...) at src/event/modules/ngx_epoll_module.c:901
#7  ngx_process_events_and_timers (...) at src/event/ngx_event.c:248
#8  ngx_worker_process_cycle (...) at src/os/unix/ngx_process_cycle.c:721
#9  ngx_spawn_process (...) at src/os/unix/ngx_process.c:199
#10 ngx_start_worker_processes (...) at src/os/unix/ngx_process_cycle.c:344
#11 ngx_master_process_cycle (...) at src/os/unix/ngx_process_cycle.c:234
#12 main (...) at src/core/nginx.c:384
```

**nginx symbol/offset resolution:**

```text
0x00005ad8334e4cda -> ngx_ssl_handshake.part + 90
0x00005ad8334e52a4 -> ngx_ssl_handshake_handler + 68
0x00005ad8334dccca -> ngx_epoll_process_events.lto_priv + 538

addr2line:
0x69cda -> ngx_ssl_handshake.part.0
0x6a2a4 -> ngx_ssl_handshake_handler, ngx_event_openssl.c:2561
0x61cca -> ngx_epoll_process_events, ngx_epoll_module.c:901
0x5d351 -> ngx_process_events_and_timers, ngx_event.c:250
0x6345d -> ngx_worker_process_cycle, ngx_process_cycle.c:723
```

**Register state at the crash in `memset`:**

```text
First core:
rdi = 0x5ad86cfee000
rsi = 0x0
rdx = 0x5ad865e4db34

Second core:
rdi = 0x5ad86ad0f000
rsi = 0x0
rdx = 0x5ad865e31894
```

The `rdx` value is huge and pointer-like, so I inspected the OpenSSL `SSL *` and `BUF_MEM` state from the libssl caller frame.

**Disassembly around the libssl caller shows a call to `BUF_MEM_grow_clean@participant1`:**

```asm
mov    0x88(%r15),%rdi
lea    0x4(%rax),%rcx
mov    0x90(%r15),%rax
movslq %ecx,%rsi
mov    %rcx,-0xa0(%rbp)
sub    0x8(%rdi),%rax
mov    %rax,-0xa8(%rbp)
call   BUF_MEM_grow_clean@participant1
test   %rax,%rax
```

This appears to correspond to OpenSSL growing `s->init_buf` during TLS handshake message parsing.

**Inspecting the `SSL *` and `BUF_MEM` fields:**

```text
$r15 = 0x5ad865e34200

s->init_buf = *(void **)($r15 + 0x88) = 0x5ad865e30e60
s->init_msg = *(void **)($r15 + 0x90) = 0x5ad865e4db14
```

**Dump of `s->init_buf`:**

```text
0x5ad865e30e60: 0x0000000100000200  0x00005ad865e4db10
0x5ad865e30e70: 0x0000000000005558  0x0000000000000000
```

**Interpreting this as OpenSSL `BUF_MEM`:**

```text
length = 0x0000000100000200 = 4294967808
data   = 0x00005ad865e4db10
max    = 0x0000000000005558 = 21848
flags  = 0
```

This looks corrupted because `length` is far larger than `max`. Also:

```text
s->init_msg == s->init_buf->data + 4
```

which looks normal for TLS handshake parsing. The obviously bad field appears to be:

```text
s->init_buf->length = 0x100000200
```

It looks like it may have been intended to be `0x200`, but the upper 32 bits became `0x1`.

**My current interpretation:**


The worker crashes during `ngx_ssl_handshake()`, inside OpenSSL while growing/cleaning the TLS handshake init buffer.
OpenSSL's `BUF_MEM` metadata is already corrupted at the time of the crash:
length = `0x100000200` while max = `0x5558`.
`BUF_MEM_grow_clean()` then reaches `zmemset()` with an absurd length and the worker segfaults.


Because disabling QUIC and fully restarting nginx made Active connections stable, and because this started after moving from 1.28.x to 1.30.x, this looks like a nginx 1.30.x HTTP/3/QUIC/OpenSSL interaction issue rather than a normal connection leak.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed follow-up -- the coredumps settle it, and they confirm my earlier hypothesis #2 (crashed workers, not a real leak).

**Root cause:** same crash as #1490 -- identical stack (`BUF_MEM_grow_clean` -> `memset` inside `SSL_do_handshake`, via `ngx_ssl_handshake`), same 1.30.x + OpenSSL 3.0.13 + Ubuntu 24.04, same "disable QUIC and it stops." The fault is inside OpenSSL's own handshake code, reached through the **OpenSSL 3.0-3.4 QUIC compatibility layer**; nginx is just making a standard API call.

**Why Active climbs:** each segfault leaves that worker's connection counts un-decremented in the shared stub_status zone, cleared only by a full restart -- exactly your "creeps up, `worker_shutdown_timeout` doesn't help, only a restart resets it" pattern. A side-effect of the crashes, not a separate leak.

I also tried to reproduce it under AddressSanitizer (thousands of oversized-ClientHello QUIC + concurrent TCP TLS handshakes) and, like the maintainer in #1490, couldn't trigger it synthetically -- consistent with an OpenSSL-internal bug that only surfaces under real traffic.

**Fix** (as in #1490): build against **OpenSSL 3.5.1+** (native QUIC API, no compat layer), or **disable HTTP/3** on OpenSSL 3.0-3.4 builds.

Closing as a duplicate of #1490 -- please follow that issue for updates.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Small clarification that changes the answer: the nginx.org Noble package doesn't ship its own OpenSSL -- it links the **system** one, which on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is 3.0.13 and stays on 3.0.x for the life of the LTS. So yes, that package keeps using OpenSSL 3.0.x and therefore the QUIC compatibility layer; it won't change that on its own.

Two things to keep in perspective:
- It's not broken for normal TLS -- HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 on the same OpenSSL are fine. Only the HTTP/3 handshake (via the compat layer) hits this.
- A real code fix has to come from OpenSSL -- the crash is inside its own handshake code. That's why nginx recommends OpenSSL 3.5.1+ for QUIC (native API, no compat layer).

So your options:
- **Stay on the stock package, disable HTTP/3** -- the compat layer is never exercised and the crashes stop (what you already saw). Clients just use HTTP/2.
- **Build against OpenSSL 3.5.1+** (or BoringSSL/QuicTLS) if you want HTTP/3 -- a custom build, since the Noble package tracks system OpenSSL.

On a 24.04 LTS box that wants the official package, disabling HTTP/3 is the pragmatic choice until you're on a base with OpenSSL 3.5.1+.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
3.0-3.4 nginx implements the QUIC API itself (src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_openssl_compat.c), feeding hand-built TLS
  records into OpenSSL's TLS stack; on 3.5+ that shim isn't compiled and the native API is used.

  So I audited that path (SSL_provide_quic_data -> ngx_quic_compat_create_record). The framing buffers are correctly
  bounded (no overflow), and the one heap-relevant compat bug -- a NULL-context deref when key setup fails under memory
  pressure -- was already fixed (c67bf9415, present in 1.30.2/1.30.3). I don't find an nginx-side defect that would
  corrupt OpenSSL's heap.

  That said, "it's inside OpenSSL" isn't settled either: this is heap corruption (BUF_MEM length 0x100000200), so the
  crash in SSL_do_handshake() is a delayed victim, not necessarily the origin -- and "3.5+ fixes it" is a confound,
  since upgrading swaps the OpenSSL version and nginx's code path at once. I also couldn't reproduce it under ASAN with
  synthetic load, same as the maintainer in #1490; it only appears under sustained real traffic.

  Disabling the shim is effectively "disable HTTP/3 on 3.0-3.4," which is the existing recommendation and would drop
  HTTP/3 for every current LTS. Remediation is unchanged: OpenSSL 3.5.1+ for QUIC, or disable HTTP/3 on 3.0-3.4 builds.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
synthetic load didn't do it for me or for the maintainer in #1490, so it needs a build running where the crash
  actually happens. If anyone still hitting this (e.g. @reporter) can run an ASAN build for a bounded window under real
  traffic, it would capture the origin.

  Recipe -- add to your existing configure line, keeping --with-http_v3_module and system OpenSSL 3.0.x as-is:
```
  ./configure ... \
      --with-cc-opt="-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O1" \
      --with-ld-opt="-fsanitize=address"
  make -j$(nproc)
```
  Run it where it crashes, with ASAN set to log the first fault (via the systemd unit's Environment= or your start
  command -- the env must reach the worker processes):

  ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:log_path=/var/log/nginx/asan:print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1

  Expect ~2-3x CPU/memory, so a short representative window is enough. What to grab: the first /var/log/nginx/asan.<pid>
  file containing ERROR: AddressSanitizer -- that stack shows who made the bad write. ASAN instruments OpenSSL's
  allocations too (even though libcrypto itself isn't built with it), so a cross-object overflow gets caught at the
  write and pins the origin to either nginx's shim or OpenSSL.

  One honest caveat so a null result isn't over-read: the corrupted value (BUF_MEM length 0x100000200 -- a small value
  with a stray high 32 bits) looks like an in-place wrong-value write inside a valid allocation, which ASAN does not
  catch (it only flags out-of-bounds access). So a hit is decisive; but if workers still crash with no ASAN report, that
  itself points at an in-struct write inside OpenSSL, and the next step would be a UBSan build of OpenSSL to catch the
  bad arithmetic.
